10.1116/6.0005690.abstract: This study investigates the use of pinacolborane as a small molecule inhibitor for the area selective atomic layer deposition (ALD) of Ru on oxide, nitride, and metal surfaces. Pinacolborane selectively chemisorbs and blocks the Ru film growth on native SiO2, TiN, Co, Cu, HfO2, and ZrO2 surfaces while Ru film grows solely on a Pt surface. The surfaces were subjected to eight exposures of 10 s pulses of pinacolborane separated by 30 s of N2 purging, followed by Ru film deposition with bis(cyclopentadienyl)ruthenium (RuCp2) and O2 at 340 °C. The process was tested at various temperatures, and the difference between the growth surface and nongrowth surfaces was the most evident at 340 °C. Energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy confirmed the selective deposition of Ru film on Pt surfaces. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed the presence of boron on the HfO2 surface after the pinacolborane exposures. Selectivity of the Ru growth on Pt is greater than 0.9 with respect to native SiO2 up to 300 Ru ALD cycles; TiN, HfO2, and ZrO2 up to 900 Ru ALD cycles; Co up to 700 Ru ALD cycles; and Cu up to 1000 Ru ALD cycles. Additionally, in an ABC-type process where pinacolborane is dosed in every ALD cycle, Ru film grows only on Ru while being effectively suppressed on native SiO2 and Pt surfaces. Our findings can serve as a valuable resource in the fabrication of next-generation interconnects.

10.1142/s0219455428500150.abstract: This paper investigates dynamic behavior and frequency characteristics of a nanocomposite curved beam subjected to two different cases of thermal shock loads. The structure is made of hybrid dual-FG (functionally graded) composite materials reinforced by GNPs (graphene nanoplatelets). The nanocomposite curved beam with different cases of end conditions is also supported by a two-parameter elastic substratum. The Halpin–Tsai procedure and the Voigt micromechanical rule are used to calculate the equivalent material characteristics of the nanocomposite media as a combination of the polymeric matrix and GNPs. The kinematic equations of the suddenly heated curved beam are established based on the Timoshenko theory by considering the von–Karman assumptions. The nonlinear equations of motion are also obtained for the nanocomposite curved beam supported over an elastic foundation using the energy principle of Hamilton. The system of equations of motion as well as the heat conduction problem is solved numerically utilizing the GDQ approach and also the Crank–Nicolson technique for three different cases of boundary conditions and also two different cases of thermal shock loads. A frequency analysis is also performed. After validation, several graphical examples are provided to estimate the thermally induced vibration response of the dual-FG nanocomposite curved beam. This study has theoretical value for the optimization of mechanical lightweight structures and intelligent thermal management.

10.1186/s12934-026-03118-3.abstract: Abstract Background Alkylamine production depends on ammonium produced via the energy-intensive, fossil-based Haber-Bosch process. Diazotrophic bacteria could offer a biological alternative by supplying nitrogen directly from air to heterotrophic whole-cell biocatalysts for alkylamine production. However, their integration with yeast production systems remains largely unexplored. Results Here, we evaluated the use of an ammonium-excreting strain of Azotobacter vinelandii (AZBB664) to supply nitrogen to an engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae biocatalyst for vanillylamine production using air as the sole nitrogen source. A modified Burk’s medium was developed to support S. cerevisiae growth and enable evaluation of biologically supplied nitrogen. Co-cultivation of both organisms was feasible under diazotrophic conditions, however, vanillin oxidation by A. vinelandii prevented effective vanillylamine production. To address this, a sequential process was implemented in which A. vinelandii was first used to generate ammonium in a modified Burk’s medium, followed by cell removal and use of the resulting medium (AZM1) for yeast cultivation. In this medium, the yeast strain CEN.PK 113-7d exhibited a growth rate of 0.27 h − 1 and reached higher final cell density compared to the control medium supplemented with synthetic ammonium. Cultivation in AZM1 was associated with a more stable pH profile, which may have contributed to the improved growth of the yeast. S. cerevisiae strain TMBNM033 expressing recombinant transaminase and alanine dehydrogenase was able to convert vanillin to vanillylamine, although a significant amount of vanillic alcohol was also observed due to competing endogenous reductase activity. Conclusions A. vinelandii- derived medium enables yeast growth and whole-cell reductive amination using air as the sole nitrogen source. This demonstrates that biologically fixed nitrogen can directly sustain heterotrophic whole-cell biotransformations, establishing a strategy for coupling diazotrophy with biocatalytic production systems.
10.1186/s12934-026-03118-3.title: Coupling bacterial nitrogen fixation to yeast whole-cell biocatalysis enables amine production using air as the sole nitrogen source

10.1364/ao.606160.abstract: Electrically controlled solid propellants (ECSPs) are promising candidates for electrically driven energy conversion systems where electrical conduction, Joule heating, phase transition, and combustion processes are strongly coupled. However, the transient evolution of the solid–liquid phase transition and its interaction with electrical energy deposition remain insufficiently understood due to the lack of effective in situ diagnostic approaches. In this study, a laser-based optical diagnostic method combined with synchronized electrical measurements was developed to visualize and quantitatively characterize the transient phase transition and combustion surface evolution of ECSPs under electrical excitation. A controlled end-face energy-release configuration was established to regulate the electrical conduction pathway and achieve localized energy deposition. The proposed optical diagnostic method enables real-time observation of molten-phase formation, liquid-phase interconnection, and surface regression behaviors during the energy-release process. The results reveal that electrical activation initially induces the formation and expansion of a molten layer on the propellant surface, followed by rapid energy release triggered by the establishment of a continuous conductive pathway. Contact pressure significantly influences the phase transition and energy-release characteristics by modifying the interfacial contact conditions and electrical transport behavior. Furthermore, the surface regression process exhibits a strong correlation with the electrical response, demonstrating the coupling between energy deposition and material regression. This study provides an effective optical diagnostic approach for investigating transient phase transitions and electrothermal coupling behaviors in ECSPs, offering valuable insights into the design and control of electrically activated energy conversion systems.
10.1364/ao.606160.title: Laser-based optical diagnostics of solid–liquid phase transition and Joule-heating-driven thermal behavior in electrically controlled solid propellants

10.1371/journal.pone.0346219.abstract: Energy cost reduction for nitrogen fixation (NF) using non-thermal plasma remains a global challenge. Researchers are exploring to reach the theoretical energy cost limit of 0.2 MJ.mol-1 for NF. A fixed grounded electrode (FGE) plasma jet has designed, studied NOx production efficiency and energy cost, and compared the results with the traditional floating water ground electrode (FWGE) configuration. The plasma was characterized by the optical emission spectroscopic (OES) technique. The experimental setup was optimized for gas composition and flow rate. The efficient gas composition ratio was identified as air:O2::5:3 with the flow rate of 3 L.min-1, and the temporal evolution of NOx production and efficiency were analyzed for both electrode configurations. For FGE, the NOx synthesis rate was 3.83 mmol.h-1 and the energy cost was 25.74 MJ.mol-1 for a 10 min treatment, and the synthesis rate was decreased, whereas the energy cost was increased with water treatment time. While for FWGE, the synthesis rate and energy cost were 1.71 mmol.h-1 and 71.5, MJ.mol-1, respectively, for the same treatment time. The synthesis rate was decreased with treatment time, whereas the energy cost was increased initially but decreased as the treatment time progresses. The promising result of this experiment is that the FGE configuration achieved a significantly lower energy cost and higher synthesis rate compared to FWGE. The proposed FGE plasma jet system might provide a way in plasma-assisted NF at low energy cost through the synergistic optimization of ground electrode, jet configuration, plasma-catalyst incorporation, gas flow dynamics, and treatment duration.

10.1515/revce-2025-0083.abstract: Abstract The utilization of CO 2 and CH 4 through dry reforming of methane (DRM) offers a promising pathway for syngas production while mitigating greenhouse gas emissions. However, its practical application is hindered by rapid catalyst deactivation due to coke formation, metal sintering, and instability under high-temperature conditions. This review critically examines recent advances in DRM catalyst design, focusing on the interplay between reaction thermodynamics, kinetics, and catalyst architecture. Ni-based catalysts, bimetallic systems, and promoted supports are discussed in terms of their roles in enhancing CO 2 activation, oxygen mobility, and resistance to deactivation. Advanced synthesis techniques, including atomic layer deposition, flame spray pyrolysis, and plasma-assisted methods, are highlighted for their ability to control metal dispersion and metal–support interactions. Special emphasis is placed on core–shell structures, where optimized shell composition and porosity enable improved stability by regulating sintering and carbon formation pathways. Overall, this review provides an integrated framework linking fundamental reaction constraints with catalyst design strategies, offering insights for the development of robust and scalable DRM catalysts.

10.17586/2687-0568-2026-8-3-159-175.abstract: Ammonia is essential for fertilizers, chemicals, and emerging carbon-free energy systems, yet its conventional production relies on an energy-intensive process with substantial carbon dioxide emissions. Photoelectrocatalytic nitrogen reduction has emerged as a promising route for sustainable ammonia synthesis under mild conditions, combining solar light absorption with an electrochemical bias to activate the inert nitrogen molecule. This review examines recent progress in this field, focusing on the design of stable titanium dioxide-based photoanodes and selective photocathodes incorporating copper oxide and two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides such as molybdenum disulfide and tungsten disulfide. Synthesis strategies, fabrication methods, cell configurations, reaction mechanisms, and performance parameters are discussed. Key challenges, including the high activation barrier of nitrogen, competing hydrogen evolution, and nitrogen mass-transfer limitations, are analyzed alongside verification protocols and future directions for efficient, carbon-free ammonia production.

As a green, pollution-free process, electrochemical nitrate reduction (NO 3 RR) exhibits extremely high application potential. However, the popularization of this method is constrained by the complex synthesis process, high cost and low stability of electrode materials. The Faradaic efficiency of Mn-Cu/NF for the electrocatalytic reduction of nitrate to ammonia reaches as high as 94% at − 0.4 V, with an ammonia production rate up to 0.82 mg h⁻ 1 cm⁻ 2 . Subsequent conditional experiments and tests demonstrate that the constructed heterojunction not only increases the electrochemically active surface area of Mn-Cu/NF, but also enhances its capacity for water dissociation and proton transport, thereby promoting the generation of hydrogen radicals and ultimately improving its NO 3 RR performance. This work provides insights for the development of NO 3 RR electrode materials with simple synthesis methods, low cost and high efficiency.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-10971029/v1.abstract: Abstract Ammonia (NH 3 ) is a dangerous gas widely used in industrial and agricultural applications, and its rapid detection is essential for environmental monitoring and human safety. In this work, Pure and Ni-doped FeMnO 3 thin films were prepared by chemical spray pyrolysis and investigated for ambient-temperature ammonia gas sensing. X-ray diffraction analysis confirmed the formation of a crystalline cubic phase of FeMnO 3 , and a slight shift in the diffraction peaks indicated the successful incorporation of Ni ions into the lattice. Surface morphology analysis revealed that Ni doping significantly modified the microstructure and increased surface roughness, thereby enhancing the number of active sites for gas adsorption. Among the fabricated samples, the 3 wt.% Ni-doped FeMnO₃ thin film (NFM2) exhibited the best ammonia selectivity of 67% at 100 ppm NH₃ at room temperature. The sensor also demonstrated rapid response and recovery times of 136 s and 94 s, respectively. These improvements are attributed to the synergistic effects of Ni- induced defect engineering, increased oxygen vacancy concentration, enhanced surface roughness, and improved charge transport. Furthermore, the fabricated sensor exhibited good humidity tolerance and good operational stability over seven weeks, demonstrating its reliability under ambient conditions. The developed sensor operates at room temperature without external heating, making it suitable for low-power sensing applications.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-11071670/v1.abstract: Abstract Photocatalytic synthesis of formamide (FA) through C─N bond construction from carbon and nitrogen-containing small molecules offers a sustainable route for converting solar energy into value-added chemicals. However, selective C─N coupling is often limited by mismatched reaction kinetics between carbon and nitrogen substrates. Here, we develop a CdS−diethylenetriamine (CdS − D) composite with an amino-confined, compressively strained interface for FA synthesis from methanol and ammonia. Local strain promotes methanol C─H activation, while surface amino groups transiently retain methanol-derived species near the interface, improving their temporal overlap with nitrogen-derived intermediates and favoring productive C─N coupling over competing pathways. CdS − D achieves an FA production rate of 8.51 mmol g − 1 h − 1 with 84.47% selectivity, 49 times that of pristine CdS, without cocatalysts or external oxidants. This work elucidates how amino confinement and compressive strain mitigate the kinetic disparity between methanol and ammonia oxidation and promote productive interfacial radical conversion, offering a viable strategy for the selective photocatalytic synthesis of value-added amides from simple molecular feedstocks.

10.21315/jps2026.37.2.7.abstract: This study investigates the structural, optical and gas sensing properties of tin oxide (SnO₂)-doped germanium oxide (GeO₂) thin films synthesised by pulsed laser deposition (PLD) on Si (111) substrates. Doping concentrations of 2 wt %, 3 wt%, 5 wt% and 8 wt% were employed using a constant laser energy of 350 mJ. The fabricated films were evaluated for ammonia (NH₃) gas sensing at operating temperatures of 200°C, 250°C and 300°C. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis confirmed that the deposited films were polycrystalline in nature. The dominant crystalline phases were identified as hexagonal GeO₂ (101) and SnO₂ (110). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images revealed a progressive increase in particle size with increasing SnO₂ doping concentration. In contrast, atomic force microscopy (AFM) analysis showed an increase in grain size distribution, surface roughness and root mean square (RMS) values as the SnO₂ content increased. Optical measurements indicated that absorbance increased with higher SnO₂ doping levels, accompanied by a reduction in the optical band gap energy. Gas sensing measurements demonstrated that the GeO₂ film doped with 8 wt% SnO₂ exhibited the best performance, achieving a maximum sensitivity of 16% at 300°C under exposure to 100 ppm NH₃. The optimised sensor also showed fast dynamic behaviour, with a response time (t_res) of 26.1 s and a recovery time (t_rec) of 34.1 s. The remaining GeO₂:SnO₂/Si samples exhibited comparatively lower and varied sensing responses.

10.2139/ssrn.7404325.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction (NO₃RR) offers a promising route for ammonia synthesis, but is hindered by slow kinetics and competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Herein, ultrathin Cu‐doped Co₃O₄/reduced graphene oxide (Cu‐Co₃O₄/rGO) nanosheets are prepared through the morphology and electronic structure modulation for efficient NO₃RR performance. Combined experiments and DFT computations disclose that Cu doping induces 2D nanosheet morphology, up-modulates the d‐band center to optimize the adsorption strengthen of reactants and key intermediates, and constructs Cu‐Co tandem sites for cascade catalysis, while rGO improves the composite conductivity. The optimized catalyst exhibits a Faradaic efficiency of 98.5% at -0.7 V vs. RHE and an ammonia yield of 25.2 mg h-¹ mgcat-¹ at -1.0 V vs. RHE with high stability. The in‐situ electro‐generated ammonia acts directly as a base catalyst for chalcone synthesis with 75.9% conversion, constructing a waste‐to‐resource‐to‐value model integrating nitrate remediation and sustainable fine‐chemical synthesis.

10.2139/ssrn.7417057.abstract: Cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE) possesses outstanding properties—including durability, chemical inertness, and resistance to flow at elevated temperatures—yet its permanent cross-linked network poses substantial challenges for sustainable end-of-life management. Here we demonstrate the rapid upcycling of waste XLPE cable insulation into graphene within 10 s via flash Joule heating (FJH) using an inexpensive (~$120) commercial arc welder. We reveal that FJH behavior is governed by the combined effects of the bulk electrical resistance of the feedstock and conductive-pathway homogeneity, both of which are strongly influenced by XLPE particle size. Specifically, XLPE scraps with particle sizes below 1000 μm promote the formation of uniform conductive pathways while maintaining favorable bulk resistance (15‒50 Ω), thus enabling complete FJH and producing higher-quality graphene. Raman spectroscopy confirms that graphene produced by complete FJH exhibits I2D/IG ratios ≥ 2 and is nearly defect-free in selected regions, and that the ground graphene products show average I2D/IG ratios of 0.80–1.12. In contrast, even at a favorable bulk resistance of ~50 Ω, XLPE scraps with particle sizes above 1000 μm predominantly undergo localized FJH because of less homogeneous conductive pathways, yielding lower-quality graphene with average I2D/IG ratios of 0.46–0.60. A comparison with a low-density polyethylene (LDPE) control further demonstrates that the permanent cross-linking network preserves the feedstock architecture and conductive pathways, enabling complete FJH, whereas melting of LDPE disrupts these pathways, resulting in lower-quality graphene. These findings establish a processing-parameter framework for upcycling thermoset waste and lay the foundation for its scalable valorization.

10.2139/ssrn.7422403.abstract: Ammonia decomposition catalysts for hydrogen release have attracted increasing attention as a key technology for achieving a carbon-neutral society. In this study, we systematically investigated the enhancement of catalytic activity and synergistic effects in ammonia decomposition by introducing alkali metal promoters, cesium (Cs) and potassium (K), individually and in combination, into Ru/CeO2 catalysts. The Ru/CeO2 catalyst co-promoted with Cs and K exhibited significantly higher ammonia conversion and turnover frequency (TOF = 0.936 s-1) than catalysts containing a single promoter or no promoter. Notably, approximately 90% ammonia conversion and excellent long-term stability were achieved at 450 ℃. In particular, the K-Cs-Ru/CeO2 catalyst showed the highest electron density at the Ru active sites, enhanced metal–support interactions, and the greatest concentration of oxygen vacancies, which were associated with an increased Ce3+ ratio. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that promoter-induced modulation of the electronic structure of Ru d orbitals and Ru-N interactions in Ru/CeO2-based catalysts can enhance ammonia decomposition activity. These combined experimental and theoretical results provide valuable insights into the rational design of high-performance catalysts for ammonia-based hydrogen production and establish an important foundation for the development of low-temperature, high-efficiency ammonia decomposition processes.

10.2139/ssrn.7422743.abstract: Electrocatalytic ammonia oxidation reaction (EAOR) offers a promising route for ammonia-nitrogen removal and energy-saving hydrogen production, yet its practical application is still limited by the sluggish reaction kinetics of non-noble-metal catalysts. Herein, a heating-rate-regulated defect-engineering strategy is proposed to construct oxygen-vacancy-rich MOF-derived NiCu oxide electrocatalysts. A bimetallic NiCu-NH2-BDC MOF precursor was thermally converted into NiCu oxide electrodes at heating rates of 1, 5, and 10 °C min-1. The optimized M-NiCuOx-1°C with a nanosheet-derived porous architecture exhibits superior EAOR performance, requiring only 397 and 516 mV to reach 50 and 100 mA cm-2, respectively, with a low Tafel slope of 23.2 mV dec-1. Post-reaction XPS reveals substantial NiOOH-like surface reconstruction, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations further demonstrate that Cu incorporation into NiOOH lowers the key intermediate-stage dehydrogenation barrier from 1.03 to 0.82 eV. In a two-chamber reactor, M-NiCuOx-1°C achieves 98.1% ammonia-nitrogen removal within 5 h and presents good stability. This work highlights heating-rate-controlled oxygen-vacancy engineering as an effective strategy for designing MOF-derived catalysts for efficient EAOR.

10.2139/ssrn.7439064.abstract: Removing carbon dioxide (CO₂) from syngas is necessary in ammonia production since the presence of CO₂ can cause poisoning of the downstream catalysts, formation of carbamates/carbondates and can add to the operation challenges. Three chemical solvents (monoethanolamine (MEA), diethanolamine (DEA) and methyldiethanolamine (MDEA)) are compared with diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (DEGDME) in this study for simulating the absorption of CO₂ from high pressure syngas from an ammonia plant. 277,792 kg/hr of sour syngas (17.34 mol% CO₂) was contacted counter-currently with 3591 m³/hr of lean solvent (50 wt% solvent) in a five-tray absorber at 70 °C and 3628 kPa and 48.3 °C and 4114 kPa, respectively. The CO₂ removal performance was compared by carrying out tray-by-tray analysis which indicated that MEA performed best due to the fast rate of carbamate formation, decreasing the CO₂ composition in the vapour phase from 0.1734 to 0.0010 mol/mol. DEA was able to achieve a moderate removal of CO₂ (0.0774) and DEGDME reduced CO₂ by physical solubility (0.0915). MDEA had the poorest performance, with CO₂ 0.1331. These absorption trends were supported by the corresponding solvent flows, which had the highest increase in loading for MEA. The results show the sequence of reactivity of primary amines, secondary amines, and tertiary amines as well as confirm that stage-wise simulation is an effective screening method for investigating CO₂-removal solvents prior to pilot-scale testing.

10.2139/ssrn.7445994.abstract: In a world committed to reducing CO2 emissions, alternative fuels such as SAF and methanol are expected to gain importance to decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors. As an alternative to the development of direct CO2 to fuels conversion processes, green syngas production can be a practical approach to accomplish this target. Reverse Water Gas Shift performed in electrified reactors represents a flexible technology, enabling the production of CO from CO2 and green hydrogen and, in turns, the application of the several available routes of the syngas platform to liquid energy and hydrogen carriers. Given the endothermic nature of the reaction and the thermodynamic requirements, high temperature heating by electrification is an open challenge. With this work we provide a detailed thermal characterization of a directly electrified SiSiC packed foam reactor loaded with Rh-based catalyst used for CO2 utilization via Reverse Water Gas Shift. The system was operated up to 5 bar, 18 Nm3/kgcat/h and 750°C achieving equilibrium CO2 conversion and CO-selectivity. Measured axial temperature profiles showed a sharp temperature increase at the inlet of the catalytic bed which was emphasized when increasing the operating pressure. This trend was attributed to the exothermicity of methanation which competes with RWGS at low temperatures and high pressures. Such interpretations were corroborated by simulation results obtained with a 2D mathematical model of the reactor which could accurately describe the observed reactor behaviour: simulated composition axial profiles confirmed in fact a substantial production of methane in the first portion of the packed foam which translated into a temperature increase.

10.2139/ssrn.7471149.abstract: Nitrogen (N2) activation and active hydrogen (*H) supply represent the major challenges in the ammonia (NH3) synthesis process nowadays. In this work, FeVO4 photocatalysts with abundant oxygen vacancies (FeVO4-OV) were prepared by a one-step hydrothermal combined with secondary annealing method. Following optimization, the FeVO4 catalyst exhibited a substantially enhanced photocatalytic ammonia synthesis rate of 43.71 μmol⋅h-1⋅g-1, surpassing that of the pristine sample by a factor of 3.4. Experimental characterizations, combined with density-functional theory (DFT) calculations, confirmed that the nitrogen reduction of FeVO4-OV proceeds via an alternating pathway, with the active center of reduction being the V site adjacent to the marginal oxygen vacancies (OVs). The valence transition of V4+/V5+ and the synergistic effect with OVs are the exact centers of activity for the photocatalytic nitrogen reduction reaction (PNRR) with FeVO4. The sustained and efficient valence transition and electron transfer of V4+/V5+ in the presence of OVs facilitates the N2 reduction reaction process. Furthermore, under the influence of OVs, Fe sites promote water dissociation to supply *H, which plays a pivotal role in the PNRR process. The synergistic effect combined with the dual sites and OVs enhances the performance of PNRR with FeVO4-based catalysts. This work establishes a rational framework for designing efficient and environmentally benign photocatalysts for nitrogen reduction.

10.2139/ssrn.7506406.abstract: Catalyst geometry strongly influences transport and reaction in ammonia decomposition reactors, but its relative performance can change upon reactor scale-up. A multiscale computational fluid dynamics (CFD) framework was therefore employed to investigate catalyst geometry effects from particle resolved to reactor scales. Unlike conventional porous medium approaches, the present model explicitly resolves catalyst packing structures generated using Blender based rigid body packing simulations. Kinetic parameters of the Temkin–Pyzhev ammonia decomposition model were estimated from experimental data using a one-dimensional (1D) gPROMS model and implemented into ANSYS Fluent through a user defined function (UDF). The particle resolved CFD results were subsequently extended to two scale-up reactor models using catalyst geometry dependent parameters to evaluate the effects of catalyst shape on ammonia decomposition performance.,Particle resolved CFD simulations showed that the sphere catalyst achieved the highest ammonia conversion of approximately 86%, whereas the 7-hole and 1-hole catalysts exhibited lower conversions of approximately 75% and 66%, respectively, despite their larger surface to volume ratios. In contrast, the scale-up simulations showed that the 7-hole catalyst achieved the highest conversion of 48.47% in the double-tube reactor, where enhanced reactor level heat transfer enabled more effective utilization of its enlarged reaction surface. This reversal demonstrates that the relative performance of different catalyst geometries can change upon scale-up as the contribution of reactor-scale heat transfer becomes increasingly important. These findings highlight that catalyst performance is governed by the coupling between reaction surface area and its thermal and hydrodynamic accessibility, emphasizing the need to consider catalyst geometry and reactor configuration together.
10.2139/ssrn.7506406.title: Multiscale CFD Investigation of Scale Dependent Catalyst Geometry Performance in Externally Heated Ammonia Decomposition Reactors

10.2339/politeknik.1820252.abstract: Ammonia has become a strategic compound for sustainable energy systems due to its carbon-free structure, high hydrogen density and compatibility with existing infrastructures. In this study, the technical and economic feasibility of green ammonia production based on the electrochemical Haber-Bosch (eHB) process is analysed in detail. Modelling results show that reactor pressure and electrolyser efficiency have decisive effects on the levelized cost of ammonia (LCOA) and operating expenses (OPEX). Under pressures above 9 MPa, the conversion efficiency and the residence time in the reactor decreases, decreasing the conversion efficiency but resulting in a smaller reactor volume, thus reducing reactor costs. Especially at electricity prices as low as 30 USD/MWh, LCOA has been observed to be competitive with conventional methods at scales above 25 tonnes/day. Furthermore, increases in capacity factor and production scale improve economic performance by spreading capital and fixed operating costs over a larger production volume The results demonstrate that high-pressure eHB systems supported by renewable sources offer an industrially viable and competitive option for decentralised green ammonia production across various sectors, from the fertiliser industry to hydrogen carrier applications.
10.2339/politeknik.1820252.title: Techno-Economic Optimization of a Decentralized, Small-Scale Electrochemical Haber-Bosch Process for Green Ammonia Production

10.26434/chemrxiv.15008158/v1.abstract: Area-selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD) of SiO 2 -on-SiO 2 requires passivating adjacent SiN to isolate charge-trap nitride in 3D-NAND. We hypothesize that a smallmolecule electrophilic inhibitor chemoselectively acylates SiN surface amines (–NH 2 /–NH) over SiO 2 silanols (–OH), capping SiN against oxide nucleation. We build an in-silico AI co-scientist that (i) constructs amorphous a-SiO 2 /aSiN surfaces validated against diffraction and calibrates their reactive-site density to experiment, (ii) benchmarks its own methods, (iii) agentically screens inhibitors, and (iv) validates against a published positive control. The core selectivity is kinetic: reaction thermodynamics are near-degenerate, but acylation strongly favors the SiN amine over the SiO 2 silanol (gas-phase barrier difference ∼0.9 eV, a stepwise addition; xTB and DFT concur on the direction), reproducing textbook amine≫silanol chemose-lectivity. With a first-principles cap oxidative-initiation barrier (Ea≈0.68 eV ⇒ kdeg≈2.9× 10 −2 /cycle), a mechanistic multi-cycle model then demonstrates the target rather than assuming it: a re-passivation supercycle (redose every 3 cycles) reaches S = 0.91 at 10 nm. Run as a genuine closed loop, the agent autonomously proposes and screens candidates, inventing a novel lead that beats a naive electrophilicity-only baseline by 2.5 eV of selectivity. Our pipeline independently reproduces the published aminosilane oxide-preference (BDIPADS), anchoring the method. The pipeline is built entirely on open-source software.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15008447/v1.abstract: Green ammonia production will be crucial to achieving global net-zero emissions. The current dominant technology for producing ammonia, known as the Haber-Bosch process, requires extreme temperatures and pressures. One promising alternative is mechanocatalysis, where mechanical energy is used to promote reactivity and reduce energy consumption. Ammonia production via mechanocatalysis has recently been demonstrated at the laboratory scale. A deeper understanding of the kinetics and mechanism of this reaction is necessary to facilitate scale-up of this process. However, this is challenging to obtain inside ball mills, the most commonly used devices for mechanocatalysis. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations to study mechanocatalytic ammonia production. A reactive force field is employed to investigate the effect of applied stress on nitrogen dissociation and hydrogenation on an iron catalyst. We find that the activation energy of the nitrogen dissociation step decreases from 56 kJ/mol in the thermally activated process on Fe(111), to 29 kJ/mol under a normal stress of 5 GPa. For the less reactive Fe(110) surface, the reduction is even more significant, from 117 kJ/mol to 35 kJ/mol. The larger activation volume for Fe(110) than Fe(111) is due to deeper penetration of the nitrogen molecules into the more open surface. The hydrogenation step was also accelerated under applied stress, although the effect was less pronounced than for nitrogen dissociation. These trends are quantified using SATA equation framework, providing the first SATA analysis of mechanochemical ammonia synthesis. We also reveal the atomic-scale mechanism of this stress-enhanced reactivity, which does not require increased defect density in the iron catalyst. The mechanistic analysis reveals that normal stress promotes Fe–N bond formation, which weakens the N–N bond and lowers the activation barrier. This is distinct from non-catalytic mechanochemistry, where normal stress typically inhibits bond-breaking reactions. Nitrogen dissociation can be further accelerated by the application of shear stress, which can promote the reaction at room temperature. These results provide an improved fundamental understanding that could help to guide further improvements in the efficiency of mechanochemical ammonia production.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15008447/v1.title: Reactive Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Mechanochemical Ammonia Production

10.26434/chemrxiv.15008494/v1.abstract: Optical fiber chemistry (OFC) is a catalytic platform in which optical fibers actively provide photon transport, interface construction, and process control. This article develops an optical fiber membrane electrode (OFME) framework encompassing architecture, mechanisms, process intensification, and programmable control. Its anode fiber catalytic layer–ion-exchange membrane–cathode fiber catalytic layer sandwich couples internal photon transport, charge transfer, ion conduction, catalytic sites, and fluid-phase mass transport within one membrane-electrode reaction domain. Equation-driven simulations examine model consistency and reactor design trends. A normalized separation of 0.1338 gives a coplanar factor of 0.882; first-order kinetics with a rate constant of 0.0568 min−1 gives 96.69% conversion after 60 min. At a dimensionless axial attenuation of 1, double-ended illumination increases the optical uniformity index from 0.712 to 0.963; at an attenuation of 3, the corresponding values are 0.186 and 0.721. Normalized rate scenarios of 1.00/1.45/2.35 generate distinct kinetic profiles for conventional electrolysis, externally illuminated photo-assisted electrolysis, and embedded OFME architectures. Interfacial chemistry, bubble coverage, membrane transport, energy efficiency, and scale-up are discussed for hydrogen and oxygen evolution, carbon dioxide reduction, and nitrogen reduction. An artificial-intelligence-assisted closed-loop framework treats light intensity, wavelength, potential, current, flow rate, temperature, and pH as executable reaction-engineering variables. OFC thus integrates internal light delivery, membrane-electrode reactions, catalytic process intensification, and digital control in a modularly scalable reaction platform.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15008494/v1.title: Optical fiber chemistry for catalysis: a programmable optical fiber membrane electrode platform for reaction chemistry and engineering

10.26434/chemrxiv.15009198/v1.abstract: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) offer molecular precision, yet their catalytic function is often treated as though the metal center operates independently of the scaffold that surrounds it. Here, we introduce TU-24, a one-dimensional COF in which phenanthroline pockets, ethynyl bridges, and pyrene cores are deliberately integrated to co-program coordination geometry, frontier electronic structure, and reaction progression for nitrate-to-ammonia electrosynthesis. Molecular deconstruction reveals noninterchangeable functions: the pyrene core supplies frontier-accessible π states, the ethynyl linkage preserves electronic communication, and the phenanthroline motif tunes the near-Fermi-level manifold while creating an accessible N,N coordination pocket. Postsynthetic Cu incorporation preserves the crystalline architecture while generating spatially dispersed, approximately four-coordinate Cu–N/O sites electronically distinct from metallic Cu and bulk copper oxides. TU-24-Cu delivers 92.0% NH3 Faradaic efficiency at −0.7 V versus RHE and an areal NH3 yield of 1.71 mg h-1 cm-2 at −0.8 V, while strongly suppressing nitrite release. Operando ATR-SEIRAS and density functional theory converge on a deep-reduction pathway involving hydrogenated N–O intermediates, with the framework favoring the lower-energy *NHO channel and adaptively weakening Cu–N binding as hydrogenation advances. These findings establish a broader design principle: COF electrocatalysis can be programmed not merely by installing an active site, but by electronically wiring that site to a framework that governs intermediate retention, pathway branching, and forward continuity across a multielectron reaction network.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15009198/v1.title: Cooperative Electronic Programming by Phenanthroline Pockets, Ethynyl Bridges, and Pyrene Cores in a One-Dimensional Covalent Organic Framework for Chemoselective Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electrosynthesis

10.26434/chemrxiv.15009355/v1.abstract: The selectivity of electrocatalytic nitrite reduction to hydroxylamine is governed by multiple coupled steps within the multi-electron nitrogen–oxygen reduction network, which cannot be represented simultaneously by a volcano relation based on a single adsorption descriptor. To address this limitation, a catalyst discovery workflow coupling machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) is developed. A small set of physical descriptors maps discrete oxide–dopant candidates onto a low-dimensional continuous representation, while four thermodynamic objectives describe the competing steps in NH2OH formation. The MLIP provides unified, low-cost structural and energy evaluation for oxide candidates. A Gaussian process surrogate model together with expected hypervolume improvement sequentially selects candidates from the discrete pool and updates the Pareto front within a fixed evaluation budget. The workflow integrates chemical objectives, energy evaluation, and sequential decision-making for catalyst screening in oxide systems.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15009355/v1.title: A Catalyst Discovery Workflow Coupling MLIP with MOBO for Nitrite-to-Hydroxylamine Electroreduction

10.26434/chemrxiv.15009696/v1.abstract: Keywords: Joule heating; Complex hydrocarbon mixtures; Light olefins; Spatiotemporal reactor; Reaction-separation mechanism Introduction Light olefins are essential building blocks for the chemical industry, and expanding their production from diverse hydrocarbon mixtures is important for improving resource utilization and securing olefin supply. Complex carbonaceous resources, including waste plastics, petroleum, and coal liquefaction products, represent abundant feedstocks for light olefin production. Industrially, light olefins are produced mainly through steam cracking and catalytic pyrolysis.1, 2, 3 These processes rely heavily on fossil fuel combustion for heat supply, resulting in high energy consumption and carbon emissions.4 It poses a major challenge to the low-carbon transition of olefin production technology. Thus, developing low-carbon heat supply strategies while maintaining high olefin selectivity is critical for next-generation olefin production technologies.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15009696/v1.title: Selective Olefin Production from Complex Hydrocarbons via Pulsed Joule Heating

10.26599/nr.2026.94908724.abstract: Abstract Single-atom catalysts (SACs) with a TM-N4-C structure, where a transition metal (TM) atom is embedded in nitrogen-doped graphene, have emerged as promising electrocatalysts for electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (eNRR). However, their performance is often limited by weak N2 adsorption and insufficient activation of the inert N≡N bond. In this work, we propose a novel bilayer catalyst architecture, Mn-N4-C/MoS2-TM, by vertically integrating the Mn-N4-C site with sulfur vacancies (Vs) on the MoS2 basal plane, where TM dopants are anchored at the Vs sites (denoted as MoS2-TM). Using first-principles simulations, we investigated the eNRR performance within the interlayer space of this hybrid system. Our results reveal that the confined interlayer region with the dual active site of Mn-N4-C and MoS2-TM acts as an efficient nano-reactor, working synergistically to enhance N2 adsorption and activation. Notably, during catalysis, the active site dynamically shifts between the Mn-N4-C and MoS2-TM sites for binding key reaction intermediates, significantly lowering the energy barrier of the potential-determining step, thereby promoting the conversion of N2 to NH3. Mechanistic analyses identify Mn-N4-C/MoS2-TM (TM = Mn, Tc, and Ag) as particularly promising eNRR catalysts, exhibiting a low limiting potential of −0.3 V and a maximum kinetic barrier of 0.75 eV. Furthermore, we developed a novel descriptor, φ=θd×XTM, based solely on intrinsic material properties (i.e., the number of d electrons ( θd) and the electronegativity ( XTM)) of the TM dopants, which accurately predict eNRR activity across the series. This work presents a unique strategy for rational design of dual site catalysts, opening a new avenue for efficient eNRR electrocatalysts.
10.26599/nr.2026.94908724.title: Interlayer-confined dual sites in a doped graphene/MoS 2 bilayer: Synergistic effects and active site switching for boosted electrochemical nitrogen reduction

10.26599/nr.2026.94908854.abstract: Abstract Constructing photocatalysts decorated with atomically dispersed metal species (ADMs) represents a pivotal strategy to maximize atom utilization and tailor active sites for efficient carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction. However, conventional synthesis strategies, typically relying on tedious wet-chemistry or prolonged thermal calcination, often suffer from slow kinetics that inevitably drive the thermodynamic aggregation of metastable single atoms or nanoclusters into less active nanoparticles. Herein, we bypassed these limitations by developing a facile flash Joule heating (FJH) strategy to engineer stable Cu ADMs on TiO2 via an ultrafast and millisecond-scale heating-quenching process. This non-equilibrium thermal shock effectively stabilizes the metal species before thermal diffusion can occur, ensuring a robust metal–support interaction, as unambiguously confirmed by aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) analyses. Consequently, the optimized Cu1.0/TiO2 delivers an approximately 10-fold enhancement in CO evolution compared to pristine TiO2 under simulated solar irradiation. Comprehensive in-situ diffuse reflectance Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) and photoelectrochemical measurements reveal that these isolated Cu sites function as superior electron-trapping centers, which significantly accelerate interfacial charge transfer kinetics and promote the activation of critical reaction intermediates. This work establishes FJH as a versatile and scalable platform for overcoming the stability-dispersion trade-off in the rational design of high-performance photocatalysts.
10.26599/nr.2026.94908854.title: Engineering of atomically dispersed Cu on TiO 2 via flash Joule heating for solar-driven CO 2 reduction

10.26599/nr.2026.94908963.abstract: Abstract Plasmonic nanotubes are promising for photocatalysis due to their hollow structure, strong light–matter coupling, enhanced scattering, short charge paths, and abundant active sites. However, their synthesis is challenging, with few reports. Uniform CuxSbyS nanotubes and CuxSbyS/Cu dual-plasmonic heteronanostructures were synthesized via direct colloidal hot-injection by controlling reaction parameters. In ammonia borane methanol dehydrogenation, the heterostructure achieves a hydrogen production rate (690.17 mmolH2⋅gcat−1⋅h−1) 5.5× higher than CuxSbyS nanotubes (126.21 mmolH2⋅gcat−1⋅h−1) and 198.9× that of Cu nanoparticles (3.47 mmolH2⋅gcat−1⋅h−1), demonstrating stability over 10 cycles. Synergistic effects drive activity: Hollow structure improves light harvesting and surface exposure; CuxSbyS/Cu interface enables charge separation and transfer, reducing recombination; strong plasmonic absorption enhances photon utilization. Results confirm electron transfer from CuxSbyS to Cu, stabilizing nanoparticles and improving durability. Density functional theory identifies CH3OBH2NH3 desorption (not O–H cleavage) as the rate-determining step, offering new mechanistic insight. This method enables applications in solar hydrogen production, environmental purification, and energy-efficient conversion for sustainable energy and green chemistry.
10.26599/nr.2026.94908963.title: Dual-plasmonic Cu x Sb y S/Cu heteronanostructures: Efficient photocatalysts for ammonia borane methanolysis dehydrogenation

10.26599/nr.2026.94908976.abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (eNO3RR) presents an innovative approach to achieve green NH3 synthesis and mitigate environmental NO3− pollution. However, the bottleneck for large-scale application of eNO3RR is the development of efficient electrocatalysts. Herein, inspired by the structure of nitrogenase and nitrate reductase, a novel Fe-Mo-based electrocatalyst (FeMoS-O) with distinctive bimetallic Fe-O-Mo active centers was developed using FeMo2S4 as the precursor via in situ electrochemical activation to induce surface O-doping. Combining comprehensive in situ characterizations and theoretical calculation results reveal that the Fe and Mo sites of the Fe-O-Mo center are responsible for the hydrogenation of NOx species and the dissociation of H2O, respectively, which is similar to the working mechanism of nitrate reductase. Meanwhile, O-doping on the Fe-O-Mo surface significantly reduces the energy barriers of the rate-determining steps of these two processes. As feedback, the synergistic effect of Mo and Fe sites endows the resultant FeMoS-O with excellent eNO3RR performance under neutral conditions, with high Faradaic efficiency (> 90%) in a potential window exceeding 0.50 V, large partial current density and yields, as well as quite good stability towards NH3 production. This work provides new insights into the preparation of more advanced enzyme-mimicking catalysts.
10.26599/nr.2026.94908976.title: Fe-Mo-catalyzed nitrate reduction: A biomimetic approach to green ammonia production

10.26599/nr.2026.94909048.abstract: Abstract Lightweight, broadband, and highly efficient electromagnetic wave absorbers (EWAs) are increasingly demanded, yet their development remains constrained by conventional equilibrium synthesis, which limits access to the high-energy structural states required for efficient electromagnetic attenuation. Flash Joule Heating (FJH), featuring rapid electrothermal heating followed by instantaneous quenching, provides an effective route to stabilize kinetically trapped structures that are difficult to obtain through traditional processing. This review presents FJH as a platform for non-equilibrium state engineering rather than simply an ultrafast synthesis technique. By interrupting thermodynamic relaxation, FJH preserves metastable phases, abundant defects, fragmented conductive networks, and complex heterointerfaces, thereby creating multiple pathways for electromagnetic energy dissipation. These non-equilibrium characteristics offer promising solutions to persistent challenges in EWAs, including conductivity-impedance imbalance, limited polarization centers, weak interfacial dissipation, and insufficient high-frequency magnetic response. The review further discusses emerging opportunities enabled by FJH, such as kinetic-state programming, structural genome engineering, adaptive electromagnetic materials, AI-assisted materials design, and scalable manufacturing. Finally, the key challenges that remain in achieving predictive and controllable non-equilibrium materials design are outlined. More importantly, FJH is highlighted as a strategy for writing programmable non-equilibrium states, opening new directions for the design of next-generation EWAs.
10.26599/nr.2026.94909048.title: Unlocking the potential of Flash Joule Heating for advanced electromagnetic wave absorbers: A non-equilibrium perspective

10.26599/nr.2026.94909059.abstract: Abstract Photocatalytic reduction of nitrite (NO2−) to ammonia (NH3) presents a sustainable path for wastewater remediation and nitrogen resource recovery. However, the sluggish seven-proton/six-electron (7H+/6e−) transfer kinetics and the formidable energy barrier of hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) limit its practical efficiency. Herein, we report a robust photocatalyst comprising quaternary medium entropy alloy (MEA) nanoparticles (Cu, Co, Ni, Zn) anchored on TiO2 nanosheets (TNS), featuring a tailor-made crystalline/amorphous heterointerfaces. The unique interfacial architecture synergistically optimizes the bidentate adsorption of nitrite and accelerates water dissociation, thereby lowering the activation energy for active hydrogen (*H) generation. Benefiting from the high-entropy-induced “sluggish diffusion” effect, the amorphous domains exhibit exceptional structure stability against photo-induced recrystallization. Consequently, the HH-CCNZ@TNS catalyst achieves a remarkable NH3 production efficiency of 99.69% with near 100% selectivity, maintaining superior durability over multiple cycles. This work underscores the potential of entropy engineering in coordinating multi-step proton/electron dynamics for advanced energy and environmental catalysis.
10.26599/nr.2026.94909059.title: Quaternary medium-entropy nanoalloys with crystalline/amorphous heterointerfaces for highly selective and stable photocatalytic nitrite reduction to ammonia

10.26599/nr.2026.94909218.abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic NOx reduction, particularly nitrate reduction (NO3RR), has emerged as a promising waste-to-value strategy that simultaneously mitigates nitrogen pollution and enables sustainable ammonia (NH3) synthesis under ambient conditions. Among the various catalyst families, perovskite oxides (ABO3) have attracted considerable attention because their structural flexibility and compositional tunability enable precise regulation of surface electronic structure, defect chemistry, and reaction pathways. In this review, we establish a unified mechanistic framework that links the elementary processes of NOx reduction with rational perovskite design. This framework highlights how symmetry polarization, electronic structure regulation, and hydrogen management collectively govern nitrate activation, intermediate evolution, and selective NH3 formation, and discusses how these mechanistic principles are translated into advanced materials-design strategies, including cation and defect engineering, phase and spatial decoupling, and in situ exsolution of catalytically active nanoparticles. We further emphasize that practical NOx valorization depends not only on catalyst optimization but also on integrating catalyst design with reactor engineering and emerging waste-to-energy electrochemical systems. Finally, we discuss key opportunities for advancing the field through operando characterization, predictive design descriptors, standardized catalyst evaluation, and data-driven materials discovery. This review provides a unified perspective for the rational development of next-generation perovskite electrocatalysts for efficient NOx-to-NH3 conversion, with particular emphasis on nitrate reduction.
10.26599/nr.2026.94909218.title: Perovskite oxide electrocatalysts for selective NO x reduction to ammonia: Material design, reaction mechanisms, and beyond

10.32964/tj25.9.577.abstract: As the global energy sector transitions toward net-zero emissions, kraft pulp mills present a compelling opportunity to produce green fuels and achieve net-negative emissions by capturing biogenic carbon, helping offset hard-to-abate sectors. This study explores the techno-economics of integrating biomass gasification for green ammonia production within kraft mills, using KraftSIM modeling to evaluate ammonia production, steam balance, emissions, and utility impacts. The proposed design enables energy and water system integration with the existing mill and allows for a gradual scale-up without disrupting the chemistry and operation of the recovery cycle. Across five scenarios representing different biomass gasification rates ranging from 100 to 1000 bone-dry metric tons per day (BDMT/d), the process yields ammonia at approximately 0.51 metric tons per bone-dry metric ton (t/ BDMT), while generating significant low- and medium-pressure steam and hot water that offset mill utility demands. The incineration of pressure swing adsorption tail gas and ammonia plant purge gas in the power boiler reduces biomass combustion and enhances power boiler efficiency. Economic analysis suggests a net revenue potential of approximately CA$380/BDMT, which could increase with the implementation of biogenic carbon pricing. Overall profitability is strongly influenced by biomass procurement costs, electricity prices, and prevailing green fuel and chemical market premium. This work outlines a practical, near-term decarbonization pathway for kraft mills by coupling green fuel production with potential opportunities for carbon removal.
10.32964/tj25.9.577.title: Biomass gasification for green ammonia production in kraft mills

10.33730/2077-4893.3.2026.370823.abstract: Biological nitrogen fixation (BNF) is one of the most fundamental and ecologically significant biogeochemical processes on Earth, providing atmospheric nitrogen input into terrestrial bioecosystems. In the current era of intensive agriculture, where global consumption of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers exceeded 116 million tons in 2025 (International Fertilizer Association, 2025), the problem of persistently low nitrogen use efficiency (NUE 40–55%) and its severe environmental consequences has become critically urgent. These consequences include massive nitrate leaching, eutrophication of water bodies, substantial emissions of nitrous oxide (N2O) — a potent greenhouse gas, and progressive degradation of soil fertility. Despite considerable scientific advances in understanding the mechanisms of BNF, many important aspects remain insufficiently explored. These include the long-term stability and field performance of microbial consortia, the influence of climate change on symbiotic and associative interactions, the vertical stratification of diazotrophic communities in soil profiles, and the regional peculiarities of implementing microbial technologies in countries with complex soil and climatic conditions, particularly Ukraine, whose agroecosystems have been significantly affected by the ecological consequences of military actions. The aim of this review is to systematically summarize and critically analyze contemporary scientific knowledge on biological nitrogen fixation and microbial biotechnologies for plant nitrogen nutrition. The paper examines the underlying mechanisms, agronomic, ecological, and economic efficiency of these technologies, and evaluates their practical implementation prospects within the global context and the specific conditions of Ukrainian agroecosystems. The review was conducted in the narrative review format based on peer-reviewed publications from 2015–2025 indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar. Special attention is paid to recent meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and large-scale experimental studies that reflect the current state of the field. The article discusses the global «nitrogen paradox», the main types of biological nitrogen fixation (symbiotic, associative, endophytic, and free-living), the molecular basis of the nitrogenase complex, and the evolution of microbial technologies — from classical single-strain inoculants to advanced synthetic microbial communities (SynCom). Key challenges and limitations of widespread adoption are thoroughly analyzed, including high variability of results, competition with indigenous microbiota, regulatory barriers, product quality issues, and socio-economic constraints. It is demonstrated that microbial technologies possess substantial potential as a strategic tool for transitioning toward sustainable, resourceefficient, and climate-neutral agriculture. They can significantly reduce dependence on synthetic fertilizers, lower greenhouse gas emissions, enhance soil health, improve nutrient cycling, and increase the overall resilience of agroecosystems. However, realizing this potential requires an integrated approach that combines precision agriculture, regenerative practices, regionally adapted microbial solutions, and supportive policy frameworks.
10.33730/2077-4893.3.2026.370823.title: Biological nitrogen fixation and microbial technologies for plant nitrogen nutrition: mechanisms, efficiency and prospects

10.3389/fctls.2026.1920221.abstract: The dual imperatives of carbon-neutral chemical manufacturing and advanced wastewater remediation require high-performance electrocatalysts capable of orchestrating complex, multi-electron reactions. However, pristine catalyst lattices are fundamentally bottlenecked by linear scaling relations. This critical review establishes defect engineering as the definitive strategy for bypassing these thermodynamic limitations, offering a unified mechanistic framework that bridges sustainable energy conversion and environmental remediation. Moving beyond empirical material catalogues, this work systematically interrogates how localized structural imperfections—vacancies, dopants, and synergistic interfaces—act as precision atomic-scale electronic regulators. By modulating the transition-metal d-band center and triggering spatial charge redistribution, defects successfully decouple intermediate binding energies to steer reaction pathways thermodynamically. A comprehensive analysis elucidates the electronic origins of defect-mediated performance across green ammonia synthesis (nitrogen and nitrate reduction) and advanced wastewater treatment (electro-Fenton, targeted non-radical persulfate activation, and priority pollutant electroreduction). Furthermore, this review challenges the pervasive assumption of static active sites, emphasizing how operando interrogation reveals the highly dynamic, transient nature of defect architectures under applied electrochemical bias. Finally, the frontier of artificial intelligence-guided discovery and multi-defect synergy is highlighted, charting a translational roadmap from atomic-level precision to robust industrial reactor integration. Ultimately, this review elevates defect electrocatalysis from a purely descriptive phenomenon into a predictive, quantitatively guided design discipline essential for achieving closed-loop global sustainability.
10.3389/fctls.2026.1920221.title: Defect chemistry in electrocatalysis: mechanistic insights and design principles for sustainable energy conversion and environmental remediation

10.3390/app16199528.abstract: A two-stage system combining biofilm denitrification and iron electrocoagulation was evaluated for treatment of real hydroponic wastewater from soilless tomato cultivation. Biofilm reactors received sodium acetate (train A) or acetic acid (train B) at a C/N ratio of 1.5, followed by electrocoagulation with iron electrodes at 1.25 A/m2; hydraulic retention time was 12 h per stage. The biological stage removed 76.9–77.5% of total nitrogen (TN) and 94.3–95.7% of total phosphorus (TP), with elevated pH promoting phosphate precipitation with naturally occurring calcium and magnesium. After electrocoagulation, overall TN removal reached 83.6–86.7% and nitrogen speciation shifted from nitrite to nitrate dominance, although residual nitrite remained 21.9–22.1 mg N/L. Residual TN remained 96.7–126.8 mg N/L, above the 30 mg N/L discharge limit. Final TP decreased to 1.5–2.5 mg P/L, below the discharge limit. Overall TOC removal reached 96.3–97.0%. The cumulative sludge had a low volatile fraction (20.0–24.2% VSS) and was enriched in phosphorus and potassium, indicating potential for nutrient recovery. Thus, the sequential system achieved phosphorus compliance and substantial nitrogen reduction, but additional nitrogen treatment is required before discharge.
10.3390/app16199528.title: Two-Stage Reactor Technology Integrating Biofilm Denitrification and Iron Electrocoagulation for Hydroponic Wastewater Treatment

10.3390/en19184407.abstract: Against the backdrop of the global low-carbon transition, power-to-ammonia (PtA) has emerged as a pivotal direction for large-scale energy storage. Distributionally robust optimization can effectively address uncertainties in energy systems; however, traditional distributionally robust dispatch models generally suffer from over-conservatism that leads to increased operational costs, and existing PtA studies mostly focus on scenario-based adaptations of established optimization tools, lacking mechanistic and methodological innovations tailored to the electricity–hydrogen–ammonia coupling characteristics. To address these issues, this paper proposes a distributionally robust chance-constrained economic dispatch model (WMDRCC) based on the Wasserstein metric and first-order moment information, and introduces a logical mapping relationship that links hydrogen storage capacity with the operating modes of ammonia synthesis. This mechanism enables real-time optimization of the H2/N2 feed ratio, mitigates hydrogen source fluctuations, and avoids reactor instability and cost-ineffective shutdowns. Furthermore, by integrating Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), duality theory, and big-M linearization, the complex robust chance-constrained problem is reformulated into a computationally tractable mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model. Numerical results on the IEEE 33-bus system demonstrate that, compared with a distributionally robust model based solely on the Wasserstein distance, the proposed method effectively reduces system operating costs under the tested 24 h daily scenarios, while simultaneously improving renewable energy accommodation and reducing network losses, thereby providing a novel dispatch scheme for PtA systems that balances both economic efficiency and robustness.
10.3390/en19184407.title: Distributionally Robust Economic Dispatch for Electricity–Hydrogen–Ammonia Coupled Systems with Chance Constraints

10.3390/en19184415.abstract: Ammonia is a promising carbon-free energy carrier for decarbonizing existing fossil fuel power plants. However, its economic viability and life-cycle environmental performance remain uncertain across different power generation technologies. This study develops an integrated techno-economic analysis (TEA) and life-cycle analysis (LCA) framework to evaluate 50% ammonia co-firing in four power generation systems: subcritical pulverized coal (SubC-CP), supercritical pulverized coal (SC-CP), integrated gasification combined cycle (IGCC), and natural gas combined cycle (NGCC). Process models modified from National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL) simulations were used to determine mass and energy balances, while TEA quantified total plant cost, levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), breakeven ammonia price, and CO2 avoidance cost (CAC). LCA evaluated well-to-gate (WTG) CO2 emissions considering both blue and green ammonia. Results show that under the current blue ammonia price of $318/tonne, all ammonia co-firing cases exhibit higher LCOEs than the reference plants, and the breakeven ammonia prices remain below current market values. Blue ammonia reduces WTG CO2 emissions by approximately 30% for coal-fired plants and 19% for NGCC where upstream ammonia production is the major emission source. Replacing blue ammonia with green ammonia further reduces WTG CO2 emissions by 27–36% and decreases the CAC by 38–60%. These results demonstrate that low-carbon, low-cost ammonia production is essential for realizing economically competitive and environmentally sustainable ammonia co-firing in future low-carbon power systems.
10.3390/en19184415.title: Techno Economic and Life-Cycle Analysis of Ammonia Used for Power Generation

10.3390/molecules31183254.abstract: Ammonia is a cornerstone chemical for global food security and an emerging carbon-free energy carrier, yet its industrial synthesis via the Haber–Bosch process remains energy-intensive and carbon-emitting. Non-thermal plasma catalysis offers a promising decentralized alternative for nitrogen fixation under milder conditions, though the long-term structural stability of supported metal catalysts under harsh plasma environments remains a key open challenge. Plasma-assisted NH3 synthesis was investigated using exsolution-derived Co-La2O3/Al2O3 and Ni-La2O3/Al2O3 catalysts in a pulsed (1 kHz at 50% duty cycle) microwave reactor operating at sub-atmospheric pressure (2–6 Torr) and 2.45 GHz. The catalysts were prepared by reductive H2 treatment of LaCoO3 and LaNiO3 perovskite precursors, deposited onto Al2O3 pellets, triggering metal exsolution and generating metallic Co0 and Ni0 nanoparticles embedded within a La2O3/Al2O3 matrix. Catalytic performance was evaluated across a range of H2/N2 flow rates (200–400 cm3/min each) and microwave power inputs (0.6–0.7 kW average), using bare Al2O3 as a reference. Co-La2O3/Al2O3 outperformed both Ni-La2O3/Al2O3 and the Al2O3 reference under all tested conditions, reaching a maximum H2 conversion of 2.39% and a peak productivity of 20.6 μmol/gcata.h, attributed to the finer metal dispersion and smaller nanoparticle size achieved during Co exsolution from the LaCoO3 lattice. Post-reaction characterization by TEM, XRD and N2 physisorption confirmed the structural integrity of both spent catalysts. No bulk phase transformations were detected by XRD, while specific surface areas were retained above 93% of the initial one. Metals’ particle size slightly increased after plasma exposure, confirming the structural durability of catalysts. These results demonstrate that the exsolution mechanism confers meaningful sintering resistance under microwave plasma conditions, establishing exsolution-derived perovskite catalysts as a promising and durable platform for plasma-assisted nitrogen fixation.
10.3390/molecules31183254.title: Exsolution-Engineered Perovskite Catalysts for Durable Plasma-Assisted Ammonia Synthesis

10.3929/ethz-c-000805960.abstract: Direct Air Capture (DAC) is widely considered essential for achieving net-zero and net-negative emissions, yet its potential to scale to climate-relevant levels remains uncertain. Here we show that the future deployment of DAC depends primarily on early capacity expansion and growth dynamics rather than on long-term demand targets alone. Using a probabilistic technology diffusion model informed by historical analog technologies and uncertain future demand, we explore a wide range of possible global DAC deployment pathways to 2050. We find that if DAC follows growth trajectories similar to ammonia synthesis technologies and liquefied natural gas, deployment is likely to remain at the megaton scale by mid-century. However, gigaton-scale deployment becomes plausible under rapid growth and strong early policy support. Our results identify short-term capacity expansion as the most effective lever for accelerating DAC deployment and highlight the critical importance of timely policy action to avoid overreliance on future large-scale carbon removal.

10.5281/zenodo.22894743.abstract: This technical addendum establishes the streamlined operational and architectural framework for Version v4 of the primary bio-hybrid muscle actuator platform. The system eliminates unnecessary thermal management overhead and volatile computing layers, focusing strictly on the natural physiological resilience of the insect tissue: Solid-State Digital Control Integration: The biological wetware layer is entirely eliminated and replaced by a deterministic, solid-state silicon CMOS microcontroller. This controller regulates a hard-coded, three-tier Dynamic Power Gating matrix (Tier 1 ECO/Standby, Tier 2 Nominal, Tier 3 Burst) by modulating electrical stimulation and fuel valves, removing all processing latency wildcards. Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) Sensor Passivation: To ensure long-term stability within the continuous 5.0% to 7.5% ethanol fuel stream, all embedded micro-sensors (pH, temperature, ionic flux) are encapsulated with an ultra-thin, chemically inert ceramic monolayer of Aluminum Oxide (Al2O3) and Titanium Dioxide (TiO2), completely preventing chemical corrosion. Simplified Metabolism and Operational Lifecycle:The actuator operates passively within its environment without requiring active internal heating or continuous cooling. The Hypertrophic Wasp Myogenic Stem Cell line operates robustly at ambient temperatures and naturally sustains prolonged workloads up to 40°C due to the evolutionary endothenmic traits of Vespidae. During the 10-hour Operational Phase, the CMOS controller dynamically manages ethanol fuel concentration between 5.0% and 7.5%. When electrical stimulation ceases, the muscle enters a natural, passive rest state. During the 6-hour Autonomous Bioremediation Phase, standard tissue regeneration and enzymatic deoxidation (via Superoxide Dismutase, Catalase, and Glutathione) occur efficiently at standard ambient room temperature. This simplified, passive thermal design extends the structural and cellular lifespan of the macroscale humanoid actuator array to 10–15 years, matching or exceeding the reliability baseline of conventional brushless DC (BLDC) motors at a fraction of the structural complexity.

10.5281/zenodo.22942702.abstract: This dataset contains DFT-calculated adsorption energies and structural, atomic and electronic descriptors for key nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) intermediates (*N₂, *N₂H and *NH₃) on 47 bimetallic intermetallic compounds (IMCs) composed of Co, Ni, Al, Zn, V, Fe, Cu and Pt. It accompanies the article "Going Beyond the d-band Center to Design Intermetallic Catalysts for Nitrogen Reduction" (Agharezaei and Ghuman), which uses these data to train interpretable machine learning models of adsorption energy. The dataset includes 1,268 relaxed adsorption configurations, one per adsorbate placed on one surface site of an IMC, across the following files: df_N2.csv: 392 configurations df_N2H.csv: 426 configurations df_NH3.csv: 450 configurations For each configuration, the files provide: the adsorption energy (eV) orientation of adsorbate (only N₂ and N₂H) on the surface (ebd-on or side-on adsorption) upon relaxation the bulk crystal system and space group intrinsic atomic properties, Bader charges and distances of the 21 surface atoms nearest the adsorbate s-, p- and d-projected DOS band centres and integrated band sums (band fillings), both local and for the whole structure All calculated configurations are included, including those where the adsorbate dissociated or desorbed. The machine learning models in the article were trained only on intact, adsorbed configurations. README.md describes every column, and the units. DFT settings are given in the Methods section of the associated article. Please cite both the article and this dataset when using these data.

10.5281/zenodo.22957246.abstract: The ēQATOR project is developing electrically-heated catalytic reactors for the transformation of biogas (a mixture of methane and carbon dioxide) to synthesis gas (a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen). Synthesis gas, or ‘syngas’ is a common chemical building block for a variety of products, including methanol.Renewable methanol is considered an important fuel for hard-to-abate transport sectors and a key platform chemical for the defossilisation of products and services. The ēQATOR concept enables the production of renewable methanol from biogas derived from biomass residues and biogenic waste. Biogas is converted into syngas via catalytic reforming, followed by the actual methanol synthesis in a second step. To utilise as much of the biogenic carbon contained in the biogas as possible, ēQATOR has developed concepts for the electric heating of this energy-intensive process and for the integration of hydrogen produced using renewable electricity. As part of the project, an integrated life cycle sustainability assessment was conducted to support informed decision-making for both technology development and policy frameworks. The aim of this study was to evaluate the potential sustainability benefits of renewable methanol produced using the ēQATOR concepts, compared with methanol derived from natural gas and to compare different ēQATOR variants using various heating and reforming concepts, as well as different biogas substrates. Another important goal of the study was to identify optimisation potentials to determine focal areas for the further development of the ēQATOR concept. The study joined three separate, complementary assessments of the classic pillars of sustainability – (techno-)economic, environmental and social – into an overall picture and analysed them collectively to provide an integrated view of the sustainability implications associated with the ēQATOR concept. The results are considered in the context of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs). In all analyses, a common set of scenarios was evaluated, based on mass and energy balances derived from detailed process models, representing potential future variants of electrically heated methanol production from biogas and renewable electricity on a scale of 500 Nm3 biogas input per hour. The scenarios encompass two different heating concepts (resistive heating and microwave heating), two different reforming concepts (dry reforming and mixed reforming), two different biogas substrates (manure and the organic fraction of municipal solid waste), as well as two implementation scenarios (either the substrate was used for energy production prior to the installation of an ēQATOR plant, or it was spread on fields or composted). The main result obtained from the comparison of the ēQATOR systems with conventional or even improved future fossil methanol production is that methanol based on biogas and renewable electricity is associated with a significantly lower carbon foot

10.5281/zenodo.22968485.abstract: This review examines the historical development of catalysis as a fundamental chemical phenomenon, tracing its conceptual evolution from early empirical observations to sophisticated modern applications. The discussion encompasses the discovery of enzymatic catalysis by Anselme Payen and Eduard Buchner, the theoretical foundations established by Wilhelm Ostwald and Svante Arrhenius, and the development of heterogeneous catalysis through the work of Paul Sabatier and industrial processes like the Haber-Bosch method. The review analyzes key debates surrounding catalytic mechanisms, particularly the distinction between catalysts and reagents, and examines how kinetic models have been refined to describe catalytic activity. Three synthetic conclusions emerge: first, catalysis represents a paradigm shift in chemical thinking by enabling reactions previously deemed impractical; second, the interdisciplinary nature of catalysis research has driven innovation across chemistry, biology, and materials science; third, the historical progression of catalysis demonstrates how empirical observation and theoretical understanding have progressively converged to shape modern chemical engineering and industrial processes.
